extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, students of poetics and literary criticism; creators of tragedy/epic/comedy
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing and judging poetry and dramatic works (especially tragedy): how to construct plot, character, diction, and other parts to produce proper tragic effect (pity, fear, catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimesis (Imitation) as the principle of the arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and allied arts are modes of imitation (mimesis): they imitate men in action and the world by means of rhythm, language, and harmony, singly or combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat imitation as the central aim: choose what to imitate (actions, characters, emotions) and by which means (rhythm, language, song). The pleasure of poetry arises from imitation and from the human instinct to learn by likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium of imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: The medium (rhythm, language, harmony) distinguishes kinds of poetic art: e.g., flute/lyre music use harmony and rhythm; dancing uses rhythm alone; poetry uses language (prose or verse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate medium for the intended effect: if the work must rely on speech and argument, prioritize diction/thought; if on movement or music, prioritize rhythm/harmony. Examples: iambic for colloquial speech; hexameter for epic narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (better/worse/as they are)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objects imitated must be types of persons in action — represented as better, worse, or as they are. Comedy represents men worse, tragedy represents men better than in life, and some works represent them true to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to idealize, degrade, or portray realistically; this choice determines tone and genre (e.g., tragedy favors elevated types; comedy lampoons). Use examples like Homer (men better) and Aristophanes (men as they are/worse).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (narration vs dramatic presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may imitate by narration (taking another personality or speaking in his own person) or by presenting characters living and moving before the audience (dramatic representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose show (dramatic enactment) when action and immediate emotion are required; choose tell (narration) for longer scope or when universalizing events. Recognize how the same subject can be handled differently depending on manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with rhythm, harmony, and song; in the form of action, not narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or judging tragedy, check that the work is serious in subject, unified and complete in action, uses varied verbal/musical embellishments in parts, and aims to arouse pity and fear leading to catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as first principle (plot over character)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the imitation of the action (arrangement of incidents) and is the first principle and 'soul' of a tragedy; character is subsidiary because life consists in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the coherent arrangement of incidents that produce causal/probable outcomes. A finely written sequence of speeches without an artistically constructed plot will not achieve the essential tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must be a Whole (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning (nothing necessarily precedes it), a middle (follows something and has something following it), and an end (naturally follows something and has nothing following it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot's incidents form a complete causal or probable sequence with a discernible beginning, development, and resolution; avoid arbitrary starts or endings that break organic unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot magnitude (proportioned and embracable)
rubrics_metrics.description: A beautiful whole must have a certain magnitude: not so small as to be confused or trivial, nor so large as to be impossible to grasp at one view; proper length admits the sequence of events under probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a scope that can be held by the audience's memory and attention (e.g., roughly a single revolution of the sun for tragedy). Avoid extremes of tiny or unwieldy scale that obscure unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (not unity of hero)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot consists in imitating one action; unity is not simply that the hero is one person, but that the incidents form one organically connected action such that removing any part disjoints the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the plot around a single central action or conflict; omit unrelated episodes or adventures of the same hero unless they causally bind to the main action (Homer's choice of single centre as model).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity (avoid mere coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should relate what may happen according to probability or necessity, not merely recount what has happened; the best plots have events that follow each other by causal or probable relation rather than by chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so later events are the natural or probable outcomes of earlier ones (propter hoc, not post hoc). Avoid solutions that depend on accidental coincidence unless they have an air of design and internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid epeisodic plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Epeisodic plots — where episodes succeed each other without probable or necessary sequence — are the worst; they break natural continuity and are often the result of writing to please players or competitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not string set-pieces or spectacles together without causal linkage. Ensure each episode advances the central action and arises from prior incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots (role of reversal and recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple actions change fortune without reversal (peripeteia) or recognition; complex actions include reversal, recognition, or both, arising from the plot's internal structure so that later events naturally follow earlier ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for complex plots when seeking stronger tragic effects: integrate peripeteia and anagnorisis so reversals and recognitions feel inevitable and are generated by the action rather than tacked on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of the Situation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, always subject to probability or necessity (example: messenger in Oedipus who intended to cheer but causes opposite effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reversals that are rooted in the plot's causal structure; reversals that come from the action (not from contrivance) heighten tragic wonder and emotional impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate and altering fortunes; the best recognition is coincident with reversal (as in Oedipus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design recognitions that emerge from the narrative and are linked to reversal when possible. Recognitions may be of persons, deeds, or identities, and are most effective when they transform the stakes of the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene of suffering (pathos) is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, agony, wounds) that forms part of the plot and can contribute to pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes of suffering when they arise organically from the plot and serve the tragic purpose; avoid spectacle for its own sake if it does not further the action's inevitability or emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy must have six parts which determine its quality: Plot, Character, Diction, Thought, Spectacle, Song.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a tragedy by these six dimensions; in composition, address each: construct the plot first, then develop character, choose diction and song appropriately, attend to thought (the reasoning and arguments), and treat spectacle as subordinate to poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot: the arrangement of incidents; the imitation of action; the most important element and the soul of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the plot complete, unified, of proper magnitude, and driven by probability/necessity. Use reversal and recognition where apt. Plot must produce pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Character: that in virtue of which we ascribe qualities to agents; it reveals moral purpose and influences action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character must support the action: it should be good (relative to class), appropriate (propriety), true to life, and consistent. Avoid motiveless degradation or inconsistent portrayals. Character is subsidiary to plot but necessary to make actions credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought: the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; the intellectual element, where proofs or general maxims are enunciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use speeches and arguments to show what follows from the situation, to establish proofs, and to give the audience an understanding of causes and motives. Thought supports the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction: the expression of the meaning in words; the metrical arrangement and choice of words (poetic diction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose language that fits character and situation. Diction should balance elevation with perspicuity; employ appropriate metres and poetic devices, but do not let ornament obscure sense or action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Song: the musical element and chief embellishment of tragic poetry, entering in some parts with song and lyric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate choric and sung elements where they enhance emotional and structural functions. Song should be used artistically to augment the imitation, not merely as decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (one of the six parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spectacle: the visual and stage elements; attractive emotionally but the least artistic and least connected with the poetic art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spectacle as subordinate to plot and poetic craft; avoid relying on stage machinery or sensational visual effects to produce what should arise from plot and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative/structural parts (Prologue, Parode, Episode, Stasimon, Exode, Commos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into parts: Prologue (precedes Parode), Parode (first choral utterance), Episode (parts between choric songs), Stasimon (choric ode without certain metres), Commos (joint lamentation), Exode (final part with no choric song after it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these formal divisions to structure action and choric commentary; ensure episodes and choric odes are integrated into the plot's causal sequence and emotional architecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic hero type (hamartia / error rather than vice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist should be neither a wholly virtuous man nor a villain: rather someone of high repute whose misfortune arises not from vice but from error or frailty (hamartia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a protagonist whose fall elicits pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (a man like ourselves). Avoid making the hero purely villainous or entirely blameless where downfall lacks causally satisfying source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper moral direction of change (good to bad)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune in tragedy should be from good to bad (not from bad to good); it should not be merely the spectacle of a virtuous man brought to adversity (which shocks but does not move), nor the downfall of a complete villain (which satisfies moral sense but excites neither pity nor fear).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shape the plot so the hero's reversal is intelligible as resulting from error; avoid endings where vice is simply punished without tragic catharsis, or where good is unrealistically punished in a way that only shocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce pity and fear (catharsis as criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should imitate actions that arouse pity and fear; the proper purgation (catharsis) of these emotions is the aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether events and their presentation move the audience to compassionate sorrow and dread in a way that leads to purification; prefer internal dramatic causes over spectacle to produce these emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet as maker of plots rather than maker of verses
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should primarily be the maker (poietes) of plots: he is a poet because he imitates actions; even on historical subjects he is still a poet if events conform to the probable/possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize shaping and arranging incidents into a coherent plot rather than polishing isolated lines. Strong plot-making outranks purely clever versification when assessing tragic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (not mere history)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry relates what may happen (the universal) according to types and probabilities; history records what has happened (the particular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, aim to express general truths about human types and behavior through imagined or chosen incidents that exemplify universal responses, rather than limiting yourself to particular historical facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy defined (object and tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates characters of a lower type and represents the ludicrous — a subdivision of the ugly — consisting of defect or ugliness which is not painful or destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comic writing, aim to depict the ludicrous without cruelty; represent characters as lesser types for satirical or corrective ends. Recognize differences in medium and origin between comedy and tragedy.
